rows.stem: A battery supplies 0.9 A current through a \(2\ \Omega\) resistor and 0.3 A current through a \(7\ \Omega\) resistor when connected one by one. The internal resistance of the battery is :
rows.solution:
The emf of the battery is the same in both trials, and in each the emf is shared between the external resistor and the internal resistance:
\(\varepsilon = I(R + r)\)
Writing this for both connections:
\(0{\cdot}9(2 + r) = 0{\cdot}3(7 + r)\)
\(1{\cdot}8 + 0{\cdot}9r = 2{\cdot}1 + 0{\cdot}3r\)
\(0{\cdot}6r = 0{\cdot}3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\)
The internal resistance is \(0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\). As a check, the emf comes out the same either way: \(0{\cdot}9 \times 2{\cdot}5 = 2{\cdot}25\) V and \(0{\cdot}3 \times 7{\cdot}5 = 2{\cdot}25\) V.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A particle of mass m and charge q describes a circular path of radius R in a magnetic field. If its mass and charge were 2 m and \(\frac{q}{2}\) respectively, the radius of its path would be
rows.solution:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so
\(qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{R} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\)
With the speed and the field unchanged, the radius depends only on the ratio of mass to charge:
\(R \propto \dfrac{m}{q}\)
Doubling the mass doubles the radius, and halving the charge doubles it again:
\(R' = \dfrac{(2m)v}{(q/2)B} = 4\,\dfrac{mv}{qB} = 4R\)
The new radius is \(4R\). Both changes push the same way: a heavier particle is harder to turn, and a smaller charge feels a weaker force, so the circle opens out by a factor of four.

rows.stem: Which of the following pairs is that of paramagnetic materials ?
rows.solution:
A paramagnetic material has atoms with unpaired electrons, giving each a small permanent magnetic moment that aligns weakly with an applied field.
SODIUM and CALCIUM are both paramagnetic metals, so that pair is the answer.
The other pairs each contain something else. Copper is DIAMAGNETIC, with all its electrons paired, so it is repelled weakly by a field, and lead is diamagnetic too. Iron, nickel and cobalt are the three classic FERROMAGNETIC elements, whose atomic moments align in domains and produce an effect thousands of times stronger than paramagnetism.
So the pair in which BOTH members are paramagnetic is sodium and calcium.

rows.stem: A galvanometer of resistance \(50\ \Omega\) is converted into a voltmeter of range \((0 - 2\mathrm{V})\) using a resistor of \(1.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\). If it is to be converted into a voltmeter of range \((0 - 10\ \mathrm{V})\), the resistance required will be
rows.solution:
A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by putting a high resistance R in SERIES, chosen so that the full-scale current \(I_{g}\) flows when the full range voltage V is applied:
\(V = I_{g}(G + R)\)
FIRST RANGE, \(V = 2\) V with \(G = 50\ \Omega\) and \(R = 1000\ \Omega\):
\(2 = I_{g}(50 + 1000) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_{g} = \dfrac{2}{1050}\ \mathrm{A}\)
SECOND RANGE, \(V = 10\) V, with the same galvanometer and the same full-scale current:
\(10 = \dfrac{2}{1050}(50 + R') \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 50 + R' = 5 \times 1050 = 5250\)
\(R' = 5200\ \Omega = 5{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\)
The resistance required is \(5{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\). Multiplying the first resistance by five, to give \(5{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\), is the trap: it is \(G + R\) that scales with the range, not R by itself.

rows.stem: Two coils are placed near each other. When the current in one coil is changed at the rate of 5 A/s, an emf of 2 mV is induced in the other. The mutual inductance of the two coils is
rows.solution:
Mutual inductance is defined by the emf induced in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other:
\(\varepsilon = M\dfrac{dI}{dt} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad M = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{dI/dt}\)
Substituting \(\varepsilon = 2\ \mathrm{mV} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) V and \(\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 5\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}\):
\(M = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{5} = 0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{H} = 0{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{mH}\)
The mutual inductance is \(0{\cdot}4\) mH. Dividing the wrong way round gives 2500, and forgetting that the emf is in MILLIvolts inflates the answer by a thousand, which is where the option \(2{\cdot}5\) H comes from.

rows.stem: The electromagnetic waves used to purify water are
rows.solution:
ULTRAVIOLET rays are used to purify water. They carry enough energy per photon to damage the genetic material of bacteria and viruses, which kills or inactivates them, and they do it without adding any chemical to the water.
The other three do not fit. Infrared rays are heat waves and would merely warm the water. X-rays and gamma rays are far more penetrating and would pass through the water largely unabsorbed, and using them would be both wasteful and hazardous.
Ultraviolet sits in the useful window: energetic enough to be germicidal, but absorbed close to the surface so that a lamp in a flow chamber does the job safely.

rows.stem: The focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece of a compound microscope are 1 cm and 2 cm respectively. If the tube length of the microscope is 10 cm, the magnification obtained by the microscope for most suitable viewing by relaxed eye is :
rows.solution:
For a compound microscope with the final image at infinity, which is the relaxed-eye setting, the total magnification is the product of the objective's linear magnification and the eyepiece's angular magnification:
\(m = \dfrac{L}{f_{0}} \times \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\)
where L is the tube length and \(D = 25\) cm is the near point. Substituting \(L = 10\) cm, \(f_{0} = 1\) cm and \(f_{e} = 2\) cm:
\(m = \dfrac{10}{1} \times \dfrac{25}{2} = 10 \times 12{\cdot}5 = 125\)
The magnification is 125. Using the near-point setting instead, with \(\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\right) = 13{\cdot}5\), would give 135, which is why the question specifies a relaxed eye.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The variation of the stopping potential \((V_0)\) with the frequency \((\nu)\) of the incident radiation for four metals A, B, C and D is shown in the figure. For the same frequency of incident radiation producing photo-electrons in all metals, the kinetic energy of photo-electrons will be maximum for metal
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the figure is the whole discriminator. A \(V_0\) (vertical) vs \(\nu\) (horizontal) plot with origin marked 0 and four straight lines, labelled A, B, C, D above them. Describing which line sits where would state the answer, so the left-to-right ORDER of the four lines and their intercepts are deliberately withheld. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Einstein's equation written in terms of the stopping potential is
\(eV_{0} = h
u - \phi_{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_{0} = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{e}\)
Every one of the four lines therefore has the SAME slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\), which is why the graphs are parallel: the slope contains only universal constants. What distinguishes the metals is where each line meets the frequency axis, which is the threshold frequency \(
u_{0} = \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{h}\).
At a fixed incident frequency the kinetic energy is \(K_{max} = h(
u - 
u_{0})\), so the metal with the SMALLEST threshold frequency gives the largest kinetic energy. That is the line lying furthest to the LEFT in the figure, the one belonging to the first of the four metals, whose work function is the smallest of the four.
So the kinetic energy is maximum for the metal whose line cuts the frequency axis closest to the origin.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The energy of an electron in the ground state of hydrogen atom is \(-13.6\) eV. The kinetic and potential energy of the electron in the first excited state will be
rows.solution:
In the hydrogen atom the total energy of the \(n^{th}\) level is \(E_{n} = \dfrac{-13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\) eV. The FIRST EXCITED state is \(n = 2\), so
\(E_{2} = \dfrac{-13{\cdot}6}{4} = -3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV}\)
In a Bohr orbit the three energies are locked together, because the electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force:
\(K.E. = -E \qquad\text{and}\qquad P.E. = 2E\)
Hence
\(K.E. = +3{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad P.E. = -6{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{eV}\)
The kinetic energy is \(3{\cdot}4\) eV and the potential energy \(-6{\cdot}8\) eV. The signs are the quickest check available: kinetic energy can never be negative, and the potential energy of an attracting pair must be negative, which rules out three of the four options at a glance.

rows.stem: A Young's double-slit experimental set up is kept in a medium of refractive index \(\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\). Which maximum in this case will coincide with the 6th maximum obtained if the medium is replaced by air ?
rows.solution:
Inside a medium of refractive index n the frequency is unchanged but the wavelength shortens to \(\dfrac{\lambda}{n}\), so the fringes crowd together.
The position of the \(m^{th}\) maximum is \(y = \dfrac{m\lambda' D}{d}\). Two maxima coincide when they sit at the same distance from the centre, so with the medium present and \(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{n}\):
\(\dfrac{m}{n}\lambda = 6\lambda \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m = 6n = 6 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 8\)
The \(8^{th}\) maximum in the medium coincides with the \(6^{th}\) maximum in air. The pattern has been compressed by a factor of \(\dfrac{4}{3}\), so a HIGHER order is needed to reach the same point on the screen, which rules out the \(4^{th}\) at once.

rows.stem: The potential energy between two nucleons inside a nucleus is minimum at a distance of about
rows.solution:
The potential energy curve for two nucleons has a characteristic shape: it is strongly REPULSIVE, and rises steeply, below about \(0{\cdot}5\) fm, passes through a minimum near \(0{\cdot}8\) fm, and then climbs back towards zero as the separation grows, becoming negligible beyond a few femtometres.
The MINIMUM at about \(0{\cdot}8\) fm is the equilibrium separation, where the attractive nuclear force is strongest and the two nucleons are most tightly bound. It is what keeps nucleons a fixed distance apart, and hence what gives nuclear matter a nearly constant density whatever the mass number.
So the potential energy is minimum at a distance of about \(0{\cdot}8\) fm.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: A pure Si crystal having \(5 \times 10^{28}\) atoms \(\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) is dopped with 1 ppm concentration of antimony. If the concentration of holes in the doped crystal is found to be \(4.5 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\), the concentration (in \(\mathrm{m}^{-3}\)) of intrinsic charge carriers in Si crystal is about
rows.solution:
Antimony is PENTAVALENT, so it is a donor and the crystal becomes n-type. A doping level of 1 ppm means one impurity atom for every \(10^{6}\) silicon atoms, and each donor contributes one free electron:
\(n_{e} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{28}}{10^{6}} = 5 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)
The mass-action law holds at a given temperature whatever the doping:
\(n_{e}n_{h} = n_{i}^{2}\)
\(n_{i}^{2} = 5 \times 10^{22} \times 4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{9} = 2{\cdot}25 \times 10^{32}\)
\(n_{i} = 1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)
The intrinsic carrier concentration is about \(1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\). Note how far the doped crystal has been driven from the intrinsic state: the electrons outnumber the holes by more than twelve orders of magnitude.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Equal amount of positive and negative charges are distributed uniformly on two halves of a thin circular ring as shown in figure. The resultant electric field at the centre O of the ring is along OC.

**Reason (R) :** It is so because the net potential at O is not zero.
rows.context:
For Questions 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options as given below.
(A) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(B) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(C) If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
(D) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

options.label: A
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the assertion says 'as shown in figure' and names no charge sign, so the field direction it claims cannot be tested from the text at all. ONE CONTINUOUS SOLID CIRCLE with its centre marked O (a filled dot). Four points sit on the circle: A at the top, B at the left, C at the bottom, D at the right, with B and D drawn as filled dots. THE ONLY DASHED ELEMENTS IN THE DRAWING ARE THE TWO DIAMETERS through O - the vertical A-C and the horizontal B-D; no part of the ring itself is dashed. Just OUTSIDE the circle each semicircle carries a row of about nine charge signs of one kind, the two rows carrying opposite signs. The signs are drawn RADIALLY, so a plus rotated toward the horizontal reads as an X and a minus rotated reads as a short slanted stroke. WHICH semicircle carries which sign is deliberately withheld, because that alone fixes the direction of the resultant field the assertion claims. Page idx 8. [CORRECTED 2026-09-12: the previous text described the ring as one solid arc and one dashed arc. Verified wrong against this paper's own printed page at 7x - the row of radially-drawn minus signs had been read as a dashed arc of the ring.]
rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. The upper half of the ring carries the positive charge and the lower half the negative. Every positive element pushes the field at O away from itself, that is downwards, and every negative element pulls it towards itself, also downwards. The horizontal contributions cancel in pairs by symmetry about the vertical diameter, so the resultant field at O points from the positive half towards the negative half, which is along OC.
The REASON is FALSE. The potential at O is a SCALAR sum, \(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\sum\dfrac{q_{i}}{R}\), and every element of the ring is at exactly the same distance R from the centre. The positive and negative charges are equal in magnitude, so they cancel exactly and
\(V_{O} = 0\)
The assertion is true and the reason is false. The pairing is instructive in itself: at O the field is non-zero while the potential is zero, which shows that a vanishing potential does not imply a vanishing field.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The energy of a charged particle moving in a magnetic field does not change.

**Reason (R) :** It is because the work done by the magnetic force on the charge moving in a magnetic field is zero.
rows.context:
For Questions 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options as given below.
(A) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(B) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(C) If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
(D) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

options.label: A
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. A charged particle moving in a magnetic field travels at constant SPEED; the field can change its direction but never the magnitude of its velocity, so its kinetic energy, and hence its total energy, stays constant.
The REASON is TRUE and is exactly why. The magnetic force is
\(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\)
which is always PERPENDICULAR to the velocity, by the nature of the cross product. Work done is \(\vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s}\), and the displacement is along the velocity, so the dot product of two perpendicular vectors is zero. The magnetic force does NO work, and by the work-energy theorem the kinetic energy cannot change.
Both statements are true and the reason is the correct explanation. This is also why a magnetic field can only steer a charged particle, never accelerate it in the sense of speeding it up, which is the reason a cyclotron needs an electric field as well.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** In a Young's double-slit experiment, interference pattern is not observed when two coherent sources are infinitely close to each other.

**Reason (R) :** The fringe width is proportional to the separation between the two sources.
rows.context:
For Questions 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options as given below.
(A) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(B) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(C) If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
(D) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

options.label: A
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. The fringe width is \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\), so as the separation d between the coherent sources is made smaller and smaller, \(\beta\) grows without limit. For sources infinitely close together the fringes become infinitely wide, so the screen shows one uniform illumination and no pattern can be observed.
The REASON is FALSE, and it states the relationship backwards. The fringe width is INVERSELY proportional to the separation between the sources, not proportional to it:
\(\beta \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\)
Had the reason been true, small d would mean narrow fringes, which would only make the pattern harder to resolve for a different cause.
The assertion is true and the reason is false.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** An alpha particle is moving towards a gold nucleus. The impact parameter is maximum for the scattering angle of 180°.

**Reason (R) :** The impact parameter in an alpha particle scattering experiment does not depend upon the atomic number of the target nucleus.
rows.context:
For Questions 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the options as given below.
(A) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(B) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
(C) If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
(D) If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

options.label: A
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: If Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: If both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false because it inverts the relationship. The scattering angle grows as the alpha particle is aimed more nearly at the nucleus, so a scattering angle of \(180^{\circ}\), which is a head-on collision followed by a straight bounce back, corresponds to the SMALLEST impact parameter, namely zero. Large impact parameters produce small deflections, which is why the great majority of alpha particles in Rutherford's experiment passed almost straight through.
The REASON is false because the impact parameter DOES depend on the atomic number. The relation is
\(b = \dfrac{Ze^{2}\cot(\theta/2)}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\,(2K)}\)
so for a given scattering angle and a given energy, b is proportional to Z. A heavier target nucleus repels more strongly and can turn an alpha particle through the same angle from further away.
Both the assertion and the reason are false.

rows.subtopic: Coulomb's Law and Forces Between Multiple Charges
rows.stem: Four point charges of \(1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) are placed at the corners A, B, C and D respectively, of a square of side 30 cm. Find the net force acting on a charge of \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) placed at the centre of the square.
rows.solution:
Let the side of the square be a, so the centre O is at a distance \(r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\) from EVERY corner. All four forces on the central charge therefore have the same distance in their denominators, and only the charges and directions differ.
Look at the two DIAGONALS separately, which is what makes the problem collapse.
Along the diagonal AC sit two EQUAL charges of \(+1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), one at each end and both the same distance from O. Each repels the central \(+4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), so the two forces are equal in magnitude and point in exactly OPPOSITE directions, along CO and along AO:
\(\vec{F}_{OA} = -\vec{F}_{OC} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \vec{F}_{OA} + \vec{F}_{OC} = 0\)
Along the diagonal BD sit two equal charges of \(-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). Each attracts the central charge, so again the two forces are equal and opposite:
\(\vec{F}_{OB} = -\vec{F}_{OD} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \vec{F}_{OB} + \vec{F}_{OD} = 0\)
Adding all four:
\(\vec{F} = \vec{F}_{OA} + \vec{F}_{OB} + \vec{F}_{OC} + \vec{F}_{OD} = 0\)
The net force on the \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) charge is ZERO.
The magnitudes are worth computing to see that the cancellation is not a fluke of small numbers. With \(r = \dfrac{0{\cdot}30}{\sqrt{2}} = 15\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-2}\) m,
\(F_{OA} = F_{OC} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}{(15\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-2})^{2}} = 0{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{N}\)
and \(F_{OB} = F_{OD} = 1{\cdot}6\) N, twice as large. Each pair is substantial; it is the DIAGONAL placement of like charges that makes them cancel.

rows.stem: Three point charges, 1 pC each, are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm. Find the net electric field at the centroid of triangle.
rows.solution:
All three charges are equal and the centroid is equidistant from all three vertices, so the three fields at the centroid have the SAME magnitude:
\(|\vec{E}_{OA}| = |\vec{E}_{OB}| = |\vec{E}_{OC}| = E\)
The distance from the centroid to a vertex of an equilateral triangle of side a is \(r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}10}{\sqrt{3}}\) m, giving
\(E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 1 \times 10^{-12}}{(0{\cdot}0577)^{2}} = 2{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\)
The three vertices are symmetrically placed about the centroid, so the three field vectors are separated by \(120^{\circ}\) from one another. Three equal vectors at \(120^{\circ}\) form a closed equilateral triangle when placed head to tail, so their vector sum is zero:
\(\vec{E}_{O} = \vec{E}_{OA} + \vec{E}_{OB} + \vec{E}_{OC} = 0\)
The net electric field at the centroid is ZERO. Combining any two by the parallelogram rule gives a resultant of magnitude E pointing exactly opposite to the third, which is the same conclusion reached the long way round.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: Derive an expression for magnetic force \(\vec{F}\) acting on a straight conductor of length L carrying current I in an external magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). Is it valid when the conductor is in zig-zag form ? Justify.
rows.solution:
Consider a straight conductor of length L and cross-sectional area A, carrying a current I in an external field \(\vec{B}\), and containing n mobile charge carriers per unit volume, each of charge q.
The total number of carriers in the conductor is \(nAL\), and each drifts with velocity \(\vec{v}_{d}\), so each experiences a force \(q(\vec{v}_{d} \times \vec{B})\). The total force is
\(\vec{F} = (nAL)\,q(\vec{v}_{d} \times \vec{B}) \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
The current carried by the conductor is \(I = nqAv_{d}\), so for a length L written as a vector \(\vec{L}\) along the direction of flow,
\(I\vec{L} = nqA L \vec{v}_{d} \qquad\text{...(2)}\)
Substituting (2) into (1):
\(\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)
IS IT VALID FOR A ZIG-ZAG CONDUCTOR? YES. The derivation above applies to any short straight element \(d\vec{l}\), giving \(d\vec{F} = I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})\), and a zig-zag wire is simply a collection of such straight strips joined end to end. Summing the contributions VECTORIALLY,
\(\vec{F} = I\left(\sum d\vec{l}\right) \times \vec{B}\)
and in a uniform field \(\vec{B}\) can be taken outside the sum. The vector sum of the elements is just the straight line joining the two ENDS of the wire, so a zig-zag conductor in a uniform field feels the same force as a straight one joining its endpoints. Only the endpoints matter, not the path between them.

rows.stem: A telescope has an objective lens of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. Calculate its magnifying power in normal adjustment and the distance of the image formed by the objective.
rows.solution:
MAGNIFYING POWER in normal adjustment, with the final image at infinity, is the ratio of the focal lengths:
\(|m| = \dfrac{f_{0}}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{150}{5} = 30\)
IMAGE DISTANCE FOR THE OBJECTIVE. A telescope views distant objects, so the object is effectively at infinity and the objective forms its image in its own focal plane. From the lens formula with \(u = \infty\):
\(\dfrac{1}{150} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{\infty} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = 150\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The magnifying power is 30 and the objective forms its image 150 cm from it.
The second answer needs no calculation once the physics is seen: the image of an object at infinity always forms at the focus, so the image distance simply IS the focal length of the objective.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
(a) Two energy levels of an electron in hydrogen atom are separated by 2.55 eV. Find the wavelength of radiation emitted when the electron makes transition from the higher energy level to the lower energy level.

(b) In which series of hydrogen spectrum this line shall fall ?
rows.solution:
(a) The energy carried off by the photon equals the separation of the two levels:
\(E_{2} - E_{1} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E_{2} - E_{1}}\)
Converting the energy to joules, \(2{\cdot}55\ \mathrm{eV} = 2{\cdot}55 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\):
\(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{2{\cdot}55 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} = 4{\cdot}875 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 487{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{nm}\)
(b) The wavelength lies in the blue-green part of the VISIBLE spectrum, and the only hydrogen series that falls in the visible region is the BALMER series, whose transitions end on \(n = 2\).
It can be pinned down exactly: \(2{\cdot}55 = -0{\cdot}85 - (-3{\cdot}4)\), which is the transition from \(n = 4\) to \(n = 2\), the \(H_{\beta}\) line of the Balmer series.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The earth revolves around the sun in an orbit of radius \(1.5 \times 10^{11}\) m with orbital speed 30 km/s. Find the quantum number that characterises its revolution using Bohr's model in this case (mass of earth \(= 6.0 \times 10^{24}\) kg).
rows.solution:
Bohr's quantisation condition says the angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\):
\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = \dfrac{2\pi mvr}{h}\)
Substituting the Earth's mass, orbital speed \(30\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} = 3 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and orbital radius:
\(n = \dfrac{2\pi \times 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{24} \times 3 \times 10^{4} \times 1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{11}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}\)
\(n = 2{\cdot}56 \times 10^{74}\)
The quantum number is about \(2{\cdot}6 \times 10^{74}\), a number so vast that it makes the physical point of the exercise. The spacing between neighbouring levels, relative to the energy itself, goes as \(\dfrac{1}{n}\), so at \(n \sim 10^{74}\) the allowed orbits are separated by utterly unobservable amounts and the motion appears perfectly continuous. This is Bohr's CORRESPONDENCE PRINCIPLE: quantum results blend into classical ones at large quantum numbers.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
(a) Write Einstein's photoelectric equation. How did Millikan prove the validity of this equation ?

(b) Explain the existence of threshold frequency of incident radiation for photoelectric emission from a given surface.
rows.solution:
(a) EINSTEIN'S PHOTOELECTRIC EQUATION treats the process as a one-photon, one-electron collision:
\(h
u = \phi_{0} + K_{max} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0} = eV_{0}\)
where \(\phi_{0}\) is the work function and \(V_{0}\) the stopping potential.
MILLIKAN'S PROOF. Millikan measured the stopping potential \(V_{0}\) for a series of frequencies on a clean sodium surface and plotted \(V_{0}\) against \(
u\). The equation rearranges to
\(V_{0} = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{e}\)
so it predicts a STRAIGHT LINE of slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\). Millikan's plot was indeed straight, and from its slope he obtained a value of Planck's constant agreeing with the value Planck had found from an entirely different phenomenon, black-body radiation. Two independent routes to the same constant is what established the equation, and Millikan had set out expecting to disprove it.
(b) THRESHOLD FREQUENCY. An electron absorbs one whole photon, of energy \(h
u\), and needs at least \(\phi_{0}\) to escape the surface. The kinetic energy left over, \(K_{max} = h
u - \phi_{0}\), cannot be NEGATIVE, since kinetic energy is never negative. So emission is possible only when
\(h
u \geq \phi_{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
u \geq 
u_{0} = \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{h}\)
Below that threshold frequency no electron is emitted, however intense the light and however long it shines, because intensity supplies MORE photons rather than more energetic ones.

rows.stem:
(a) Define the term 'electric flux' and write its dimensions.

(b) A plane surface, in shape of a square of side 1 cm is placed in an electric field \(\vec{E} = \left(100\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\right)\hat{i}\) such that the unit vector normal to the surface is given by \(\hat{n} = 0.8\hat{i} + 0.6\hat{k}\). Find the electric flux through the surface.
rows.solution:
(a) ELECTRIC FLUX through a surface is a measure of the number of electric field lines crossing that surface normally. For a uniform field it is the surface integral of the field over the area:
\(\phi_{E} = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{A} = EA\cos\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface.
DIMENSIONS. Electric field has dimensions of force per unit charge, \(\left[\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-3}\,A^{-1}}\right]\), and multiplying by area \(\left[\mathrm{L^{2}}\right]\) gives
\(\left[\phi_{E}\right] = \left[\mathrm{M\,L^{3}\,T^{-3}\,A^{-1}}\right]\)
(b) The area vector points along the given unit normal and has magnitude equal to the area, \(A = (1\ \mathrm{cm})^{2} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\):
\(\vec{A} = 10^{-4}(0{\cdot}8\hat{i} + 0{\cdot}6\hat{k})\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)
Taking the dot product with \(\vec{E} = 100\,\hat{i}\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), only the \(\hat{i}\) components survive since \(\hat{i} \cdot \hat{k} = 0\):
\(\phi_{E} = (100\hat{i}) \cdot 10^{-4}(0{\cdot}8\hat{i} + 0{\cdot}6\hat{k}) = 100 \times 10^{-4} \times 0{\cdot}8\)
\(\phi_{E} = 8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)
The \(0{\cdot}6\hat{k}\) part of the normal contributes nothing: that component of the surface lies edge-on to the field, so no field lines cross it.

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem:
(i) State Lenz's Law. In a closed circuit, the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it as per the law of conservation of energy. Justify.

(ii) A metal rod of length 2 m is rotated with a frequency 60 rev/s about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. A uniform magnetic field of 2T perpendicular to its plane of rotation is switched-on in the region. Calculate the e.m.f. induced between the centre and the end of the rod.
rows.solution:
(i) LENZ'S LAW states that the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
JUSTIFICATION FROM CONSERVATION OF ENERGY. Suppose the opposite were true and the induced current FAVOURED the change instead. Then any small increase in flux would drive a current that increased the flux further, which would drive a still larger current, and the process would build up without limit. Electrical energy would appear in the circuit, and the source of the change would be helped along rather than resisted, with no external agent doing any work at all. Energy would be created from nothing.
Because the induced effect opposes the change, an external agent must instead do MECHANICAL WORK against that opposition, and it is exactly this work that appears as the electrical energy dissipated in the circuit. Lenz's law is the sign that makes the energy books balance.
(ii) [CBSE marking scheme: it substitutes \(l = 2\) m into \(\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}Bl^{2}\omega\) and reports \(480\pi \approx 1{\cdot}51 \times 10^{3}\) V. But that formula's l is the distance from the AXIS to the far end, and the axis here passes through the CENTRE of a 2 m rod, so the centre-to-end segment is 1 m, not 2. Using the full length overstates the emf by a factor of four.]
Take a small element of the rod at a distance x from the axis. It moves with speed \(v = \omega x\), so it contributes a motional emf
\(d\varepsilon = Bv\,dx = B\omega x\,dx\)
Integrating from the axis out to the end, a distance \(l = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1\) m:
\(\varepsilon = \int_{0}^{l} B\omega x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)
With \(B = 2\) T, \(\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi \times 60 = 120\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) and \(l = 1\) m:
\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 120\pi \times (1)^{2} = 120\pi\ \mathrm{V} \approx 377\ \mathrm{V}\)
The emf induced between the centre and the end of the rod is about \(3{\cdot}8 \times 10^{2}\) V.
Note that the emf between the TWO ENDS would be zero: both ends are at the same distance from the axis and so at the same potential, and the rod behaves as two identical sources back to back.

rows.subtopic: Ampere's Circuital Law and the Solenoid
rows.stem:
(i) State and explain Ampere's circuital law.

(ii) Two long straight parallel wires separated by 20 cm, carry 5 A and 10 A current respectively, in the same direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at a point midway between them.
rows.solution:
(i) AMPERE'S CIRCUITAL LAW states that the line integral of the magnetic field around any closed loop equals \(\mu_{0}\) times the total current passing through the loop:
\(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_{0}I\)
EXPLANATION. The integral is taken around a closed path, called an Amperian loop, and I is the net current threading any surface bounded by that loop. The law is the magnetic counterpart of Gauss's theorem: it converts a difficult field calculation into an easy one WHENEVER the symmetry of the problem lets one choose a loop on which B has a constant magnitude and a constant angle with \(d\vec{l}\). That is how the fields of a long straight wire, a solenoid and a toroid are obtained.
(ii) The field of a long straight wire at distance r is \(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}\), and the midpoint is \(r = 10\ \mathrm{cm} = 0{\cdot}1\) m from each wire.
The currents flow in the SAME direction, so at a point BETWEEN the wires their fields point in opposite senses and must be SUBTRACTED:
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{2\pi r}(I_{2} - I_{1}) = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi \times 0{\cdot}1}(10 - 5)\)
\(B = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 = 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}\)
The net field is \(10^{-5}\) T, directed along the field of the 10 A wire, which is the stronger of the two at that point.
Had the currents been in opposite directions the two fields would have ADDED at the midpoint, giving \(3 \times 10^{-5}\) T, so the direction of the currents is what decides between a sum and a difference here.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: An electron moving with a velocity \(\vec{v} = (1.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s})\hat{i} + (0.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s})\hat{j}\) enters a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B} = (0.5\ \mathrm{mT})\hat{j}\). Find the radius of the circular path described by it. While rotating; does the electron trace a linear path too ? If so, calculate the linear distance covered by it during the period of one revolution.
rows.solution:
The field is along \(\hat{j}\), so split the velocity into a component ALONG the field and a component ACROSS it:
\(v_{y} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \text{(parallel to } \vec{B}\text{)}, \qquad v_{x} = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \text{(perpendicular)}\)
The parallel component feels no force at all, since \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = 0\) for it, and carries on unchanged. Only the perpendicular component is bent into a circle, so it alone fixes the radius:
\(r = \dfrac{mv_{x}}{eB} = \dfrac{9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{7}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(r = 11{\cdot}38 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 11{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{cm}\)
DOES IT TRACE A LINEAR PATH TOO? YES. While the perpendicular component carries the electron round a circle, the parallel component carries it steadily ALONG the field direction, so the two motions combine into a HELIX whose axis lies along \(\vec{B}\).
The linear distance covered in one revolution is the PITCH of that helix, the parallel speed times the period:
\(y = v_{y}T = v_{y} \times \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{7} \times \dfrac{2\pi \times 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(y = 0{\cdot}357\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0{\cdot}36\ \mathrm{m}\)
The period does not depend on the speed, which is why the pitch can be written down without knowing how fast the circular part of the motion is.

rows.stem:
(a) Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum which are (i) also known as 'heat waves' and (ii) absorbed by ozone layer in the atmosphere.

(b) Write briefly one method each, of the production and detection of these radiations.
rows.solution:
(a) (i) INFRARED WAVES are known as heat waves. They lie just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, and are readily absorbed by most materials, where they set molecules vibrating and so raise the temperature.
(ii) ULTRAVIOLET RAYS are absorbed by the ozone layer. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs the biologically damaging short-wavelength ultraviolet, which is why the thinning of that layer is a matter of concern.
(b) INFRARED WAVES.
Production: by HOT BODIES, that is by the vibration of atoms and molecules in any warm object; every object above absolute zero radiates in the infrared.
Detection: by a THERMOPILE or a bolometer, which responds to the heating the radiation produces, or by special infrared photographic film.
ULTRAVIOLET RAYS.
Production: by SPECIAL ULTRAVIOLET LAMPS, such as mercury vapour or arc lamps, and by very hot bodies; the Sun is the main natural source.
Detection: by PHOTOCELLS, since ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to eject photoelectrons from most metals, or by photographic film.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem:
(a) Explain the characteristics of a p-n junction diode that makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.

(b) With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a full wave rectifier.
rows.solution:
(a) The property that makes a p-n junction diode suitable as a RECTIFIER is its extreme ASYMMETRY between the two directions of applied voltage. Under forward bias the barrier at the junction is lowered, the depletion region narrows, majority carriers cross freely and a current of milliamperes flows through a low resistance. Under reverse bias the barrier is raised, the depletion region widens, majority carriers are held back, and only a tiny reverse saturation current of microamperes flows through a very high resistance.
In short, the diode CONDUCTS ONLY WHEN FORWARD BIASED. Applying an alternating voltage therefore lets current through during one polarity and blocks it during the other, which is exactly what rectification means.
(b) FULL WAVE RECTIFIER. The circuit uses a CENTRE-TAP TRANSFORMER whose secondary has a tap at its midpoint, two diodes \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) connected to the two ends A and B of the secondary, and a load resistance \(R_{L}\) connected between the joined diode outputs and the centre tap.
The two halves of the secondary are always in OPPOSITE phase with respect to the centre tap, and that is the key to the circuit.
During the half cycle in which A is positive with respect to the centre tap, B is negative. So \(D_{1}\) is forward biased and conducts while \(D_{2}\) is reverse biased and does not, and current passes through \(R_{L}\).
During the next half cycle A is negative and B is positive, so the roles reverse: \(D_{2}\) conducts and \(D_{1}\) does not.
In both halves the current flows through \(R_{L}\) IN THE SAME DIRECTION, because the two diodes feed the load from the same side. An output is therefore obtained during both halves of the input cycle, which is what distinguishes a full wave rectifier from a half wave one.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem:
Explain the following, giving reasons :

(a) A doped semiconductor is electrically neutral.

(b) In a p-n junction under equilibrium, there is no net current.

(c) In a diode, the reverse current is practically not dependent on the applied voltage.
rows.solution:
(a) A DOPED SEMICONDUCTOR IS ELECTRICALLY NEUTRAL because doping does not add any net charge to the crystal. The dopant atom enters the lattice ELECTRICALLY NEUTRAL, with as many electrons as protons. When it donates its extra electron, or accepts one to fill a bond, it becomes a fixed ion in the lattice whose charge is exactly equal and opposite to the charge of the mobile carrier that was created. Every free electron is matched by a positive donor ion and every hole by a negative acceptor ion, so the totals cancel.
(b) IN A p-n JUNCTION UNDER EQUILIBRIUM THERE IS NO NET CURRENT because the two currents that flow across the junction are equal and opposite. The concentration gradient drives a DIFFUSION current of majority carriers across the junction; the depletion layer's electric field sweeps minority carriers back as a DRIFT current. As diffusion proceeds it enlarges the depletion layer and strengthens that field, which increases the drift current, until the two exactly balance. Equilibrium is a dynamic balance between the two, not an absence of motion.
(c) THE REVERSE CURRENT IS ALMOST INDEPENDENT OF THE APPLIED VOLTAGE because it is carried entirely by MINORITY carriers, and their supply is the limiting factor. The reverse field is more than strong enough to sweep across every minority carrier that reaches the junction, so raising the voltage further cannot increase the current: there are simply no more carriers available to sweep. The current is therefore set by the RATE OF THERMAL GENERATION of minority carriers rather than by the voltage, which is why it is called the reverse SATURATION current and why it depends strongly on temperature instead.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a polar molecule ?
rows.context:
Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric.

The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel.
rows.solution:
A POLAR molecule is one whose centres of positive and negative charge do NOT coincide, so it possesses a permanent electric dipole moment even with no external field applied.
Hydrogen chloride is such a molecule. The bond joins two DIFFERENT atoms, and chlorine is considerably more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons sit closer to the chlorine end. The molecule is left with a small negative charge at one end and a positive charge at the other.
The other three are all DIATOMIC molecules made of two IDENTICAL atoms. By symmetry neither atom can attract the bonding electrons more than the other, the charge distribution has a centre of symmetry, and the dipole moment is exactly zero. They are non-polar, and acquire a dipole moment only when an external field pulls their charges apart.

rows.stem: Which of the following statements about dielectrics is correct ?
rows.context:
Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric.

The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel.

options.label: A
options.text: A polar dielectric has a net dipole moment in absence of an external electric field which gets modified due to the induced dipoles.

options.label: B
options.text: The net dipole moments of induced dipoles is along the direction of the applied electric field.

options.label: D
options.text: The electric field produced due to induced surface charges inside a dielectric is along the external electric field.

rows.solution:
Take the statements in turn.
The correct one concerns INDUCED dipoles: when a dielectric is placed in an external field, the charges within each molecule are pulled slightly apart, and the dipole moments so produced point ALONG the applied field. This is true of polar and non-polar dielectrics alike, and it is why a slab develops opposite charges on its two faces.
The statement about a polar dielectric fails on its premise. A polar dielectric does have permanent molecular dipoles, but in the absence of a field they are randomly oriented by thermal motion, so the NET dipole moment of the specimen is zero, not non-zero as claimed.
Dielectrics containing free charges is false by definition: a dielectric is an insulator, whose charges are bound to their molecules and cannot wander through it. That is exactly what separates a dielectric from a conductor.
The field of the induced surface charges is also wrong in direction. Those charges set up a field OPPOSING the external one, which is why the net field inside a dielectric is reduced by the factor K and why inserting a slab raises the capacitance.

rows.stem: When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the energy stored in it :
rows.context:
Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric.

The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel.

options.label: A
options.text: increases and the electric field inside it also increases.

options.label: B
options.text: decreases and the electric field also decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: decreases and the electric field increases.

options.label: D
options.text: increases and the electric field decreases.

rows.solution:
The capacitor is ISOLATED, so it has been disconnected from any source and its CHARGE Q is fixed. That is what decides both parts.
Inserting the dielectric raises the capacitance to \(C = KC_{0}\). With the charge fixed,
\(U = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2KC_{0}}\)
so the stored energy DECREASES, by the factor K. The energy has not vanished: the slab is drawn INTO the gap, and the work done by the capacitor in pulling it in accounts for the loss.
The field also falls. The surface charges induced on the faces of the dielectric set up a field opposing the original one, leaving
\(E = \dfrac{E_{0}}{K}\)
So the energy decreases and the electric field also decreases.
The contrast with a capacitor still CONNECTED to a battery is worth holding on to: there the voltage is fixed instead, the field stays at \(\dfrac{V}{d}\), and the stored energy goes UP because the battery supplies more charge.

rows.stem: An air-filled capacitor with plate area A and plate separation d has capacitance \(C_0\). A slab of dielectric constant K, area A and thickness \(\left(\frac{d}{5}\right)\) is inserted between the plates. The capacitance of the capacitor will become
rows.context:
Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric.

The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel.
rows.solution:
With a slab of thickness t filling part of the gap, the capacitor behaves as two capacitors in series, one of air of thickness \(d - t\) and one of dielectric of thickness t. The standard result is
\(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{(d - t) + \dfrac{t}{K}}\)
Substituting \(t = \dfrac{d}{5}\):
\(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d - \dfrac{d}{5} + \dfrac{d}{5K}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d\left[\dfrac{4}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5K}\right]} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d} \cdot \dfrac{5K}{4K + 1}\)
Since \(C_{0} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\),
\(C = \left[\dfrac{5K}{4K + 1}\right]C_{0}\)
A quick sanity check on the limits: putting \(K = 1\) gives \(C = C_{0}\), as it must when the slab is no different from air, and letting K become very large gives \(C \to \dfrac{5}{4}C_{0}\), the value for an air gap reduced to four fifths of its width.

rows.stem: Two capacitors of capacitances \(2\ C_0\) and \(6\ C_0\) are first connected in series and then in parallel across the same battery. The ratio of energies stored in series combination to that in parallel is
rows.context:
Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric.

The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and/or parallel.
rows.solution:
The two combinations are connected across the SAME battery, so the voltage V is the same for both and \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}\) makes the energy ratio simply the ratio of the capacitances.
SERIES:
\(C_{s} = \dfrac{(2C_{0})(6C_{0})}{2C_{0} + 6C_{0}} = \dfrac{12C_{0}^{2}}{8C_{0}} = 1{\cdot}5\,C_{0}\)
PARALLEL:
\(C_{p} = 2C_{0} + 6C_{0} = 8C_{0}\)
Hence
\(\dfrac{U_{s}}{U_{p}} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}C_{s}V^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}C_{p}V^{2}} = \dfrac{C_{s}}{C_{p}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5C_{0}}{8C_{0}} = \dfrac{3}{16}\)
The ratio of the energies is \(\dfrac{3}{16}\). The parallel combination stores over five times as much, which is the general rule at a fixed voltage: parallel always gives the larger capacitance and therefore the larger stored energy.

rows.stem: The critical angle for glass is \(\theta_1\) and that for water is \(\theta_2\). The critical angle for glass-water surface would be (given \(_a\mu_g = 1.5\), \(_a\mu_w = 1.33\))
rows.context: A prism is an optical medium bounded by three refracting plane surfaces. A ray of light suffers successive refractions on passing through its two surfaces and deviates by a certain angle from its original path. The refractive index of the material of the prism is given by \(\mu = \sin\left(\frac{A + \delta m}{2}\right) / \sin\frac{A}{2}\). If the angle of incidence on the second surface is greater than an angle called critical angle, the ray will not be refracted from the second surface and is totally internally reflected.
rows.solution:
The critical angle for a pair of media is given by
\(\sin\theta_{c} = \dfrac{n_{rarer}}{n_{denser}}\)
For the three cases:
GLASS-AIR: \(\sin\theta_{1} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}5} = 0{\cdot}667\), so \(\theta_{1} \approx 41{\cdot}8^{\circ}\).
WATER-AIR: \(\sin\theta_{2} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}33} = 0{\cdot}75\), so \(\theta_{2} \approx 48{\cdot}6^{\circ}\).
GLASS-WATER: \(\sin\theta_{c} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}33}{1{\cdot}5} = 0{\cdot}887\), so \(\theta_{c} \approx 62{\cdot}5^{\circ}\).
The critical angle for the glass-water surface is therefore GREATER than \(\theta_{2}\), and greater than \(\theta_{1}\) as well.
The reason is physical rather than arithmetical: the closer the two refractive indices are, the weaker the bending at the boundary, so the ray must strike at a steeper angle before it can be totally reflected. Glass and water are much closer in index than glass and air, so their critical angle is the largest of the three.

rows.stem: When a ray of light of wavelength \(\lambda\) and frequency \(\nu\) is refracted into a denser medium
rows.context: A prism is an optical medium bounded by three refracting plane surfaces. A ray of light suffers successive refractions on passing through its two surfaces and deviates by a certain angle from its original path. The refractive index of the material of the prism is given by \(\mu = \sin\left(\frac{A + \delta m}{2}\right) / \sin\frac{A}{2}\). If the angle of incidence on the second surface is greater than an angle called critical angle, the ray will not be refracted from the second surface and is totally internally reflected.
rows.solution:
The FREQUENCY is fixed by the source and cannot change at a boundary. A boundary can neither create nor destroy wave cycles: whatever number of crests arrive per second on one side must leave per second on the other, or crests would pile up at the surface. So \(\nu\) is UNCHANGED.
The SPEED falls, because a denser medium has the larger refractive index and \(v = \dfrac{c}{n}\).
Since \(v = \nu\lambda\) with \(\nu\) fixed and v reduced, the WAVELENGTH must shorten in the same proportion:
\(\lambda_{medium} = \dfrac{\lambda}{n}\)
So the wavelength decreases while the frequency is unchanged.
This is also why the COLOUR of light does not change on entering water: colour is determined by frequency, and frequency is the one quantity the boundary leaves alone.

rows.stem: The critical angle for a ray of light passing from glass to water is minimum for
rows.context: A prism is an optical medium bounded by three refracting plane surfaces. A ray of light suffers successive refractions on passing through its two surfaces and deviates by a certain angle from its original path. The refractive index of the material of the prism is given by \(\mu = \sin\left(\frac{A + \delta m}{2}\right) / \sin\frac{A}{2}\). If the angle of incidence on the second surface is greater than an angle called critical angle, the ray will not be refracted from the second surface and is totally internally reflected.
rows.solution:
The critical angle for a glass-water surface is given by
\(\sin\theta_{c} = \dfrac{n_{w}}{n_{g}}\)
so \(\theta_{c}\) is SMALLEST when the refractive index of the glass is LARGEST.
Refractive index depends on wavelength: it is greatest for the shortest wavelength, which is why a prism bends violet most and red least. Among the colours offered, VIOLET has the shortest wavelength and therefore the largest \(n_{g}\), making the ratio \(\dfrac{n_{w}}{n_{g}}\) smallest.
The critical angle is therefore minimum for violet light. Turned round, this is why violet is the first colour to be totally internally reflected as the angle of incidence is increased, and red the last.

rows.stem:
Three beams of red, yellow and violet colours are passed through a prism, one by one under the same condition. When the prism is in the position of minimum deviation, the angles of refraction from the second surface are \(r_R\), \(r_Y\) and \(r_V\) respectively.

Then
rows.context: A prism is an optical medium bounded by three refracting plane surfaces. A ray of light suffers successive refractions on passing through its two surfaces and deviates by a certain angle from its original path. The refractive index of the material of the prism is given by \(\mu = \sin\left(\frac{A + \delta m}{2}\right) / \sin\frac{A}{2}\). If the angle of incidence on the second surface is greater than an angle called critical angle, the ray will not be refracted from the second surface and is totally internally reflected.
rows.solution:
Read the question carefully: the angles asked for are the angles of refraction FROM the second surface, that is the angles at which the beams EMERGE into the air.
At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, so the angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence, and
\(i = e = \dfrac{A + \delta_{m}}{2}\)
The prism angle A is the same for all three colours, so the emergent angle is decided entirely by the angle of minimum deviation \(\delta_{m}\), which is larger for a larger refractive index.
Since \(n_{V} > n_{Y} > n_{R}\), it follows that \(\delta_{V} > \delta_{Y} > \delta_{R}\) and therefore
\(r_{R} < r_{Y} < r_{V}\)
Note what would happen with the other reading, the angle INSIDE the glass at the second face: there \(r = \dfrac{A}{2}\) for every colour at minimum deviation, and all three would be equal. The question asks about the refraction out of the surface, which is where the colours separate.

options.label: B
options.text: just graze along the face AC

options.label: C
options.text: refract and go out of the prism

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says 'as shown in figure' and names no angle, so the question is unanswerable from text alone. A right-angled triangular prism drawn with A at the apex, B below it at the bottom-left and C at the bottom-right; the right angle is marked at B (so AB is the vertical face and BC the horizontal one) and the angle at A is marked 60°. A horizontal arrow arrives from the left and meets face AB at right angles. The geometry is the DATA the question supplies; nothing about what happens at AC is stated. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
First find the critical angle for the glass:
\(\sin\theta_{c} = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta_{c} = 45^{\circ}\)
Now find the angle at which the ray meets AC. The ray enters NORMALLY through AB, so it passes into the prism undeviated and travels horizontally. In the triangle, the angle at B is \(90^{\circ}\) and the angle at A is \(60^{\circ}\), so AB is vertical and AC is inclined at \(60^{\circ}\) to it.
The normal to AC is perpendicular to AC, and a short angle chase gives the angle between the horizontal ray and that normal as \(60^{\circ}\). So the ray strikes AC at an angle of incidence of \(60^{\circ}\).
Comparing:
\(60^{\circ} > \theta_{c} = 45^{\circ}\)
The ray is travelling from the denser medium towards the rarer one and strikes at MORE than the critical angle, so it will UNDERGO TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION at AC and no light emerges through that face.
Had the prism angle at A been \(45^{\circ}\) the ray would have arrived exactly at the critical angle and would have grazed along the face instead, which is the distractor the question is built around.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem:
(i) Draw equipotential surfaces for an electric dipole.

(ii) Two point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are located at \(\vec{r}_1\) and \(\vec{r}_2\) respectively in an external electric field \(\vec{E}\). Obtain an expression for the potential energy of the system.

(iii) The dipole moment of a molecule is \(10^{-30}\) Cm. It is placed in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) of \(10^{5}\) V/m such that its axis is along the electric field. The direction of \(\vec{E}\) is suddenly changed by 60° at an instant. Find the change in the potential energy of the dipole, at that instant.
rows.solution:
(i) EQUIPOTENTIAL SURFACES FOR A DIPOLE. Draw the two charges side by side. Around each charge the surfaces are closed curves, nearly spherical close in where that charge dominates, and progressively distorted further out. Midway between the charges lies the plane that perpendicularly bisects the dipole axis: every point on it is equidistant from the two charges, so the equal and opposite contributions cancel and the whole plane is an equipotential at \(V = 0\). The surfaces are everywhere PERPENDICULAR to the field lines, which run from the positive charge to the negative one.
(ii) POTENTIAL ENERGY OF TWO CHARGES IN AN EXTERNAL FIELD. Build the configuration one step at a time and add the work done at each step.
Bringing \(q_{1}\) from infinity to \(\vec{r}_{1}\) against the external field:
\(W_{1} = q_{1}V(\vec{r}_{1})\)
Bringing \(q_{2}\) from infinity to \(\vec{r}_{2}\) requires work against the external field,
\(W_{2} = q_{2}V(\vec{r}_{2})\)
and ALSO against the field of \(q_{1}\), which is already in place:
\(W_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}}\)
The potential energy of the system is the total work done:
\(U = q_{1}V(\vec{r}_{1}) + q_{2}V(\vec{r}_{2}) + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}}\)
The third term appears only once, not twice, because the work of bringing the pair together is counted from the point of view of whichever charge arrives second.
(iii) The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field is \(U = -pE\cos\theta\), so the change in going from \(\theta_{0}\) to \(\theta_{1}\) is
\(\Delta U = W = pE\left[\cos\theta_{0} - \cos\theta_{1}\right]\)
The dipole starts ALONG the field, so \(\theta_{0} = 0^{\circ}\), and the field direction swings by \(60^{\circ}\), so at that instant \(\theta_{1} = 60^{\circ}\):
\(\Delta U = 10^{-30} \times 10^{5}\left[\cos 0^{\circ} - \cos 60^{\circ}\right] = 10^{-25}\left[1 - 0{\cdot}5\right]\)
\(\Delta U = 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J}\)
The change in potential energy is \(5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-26}\) J, and it is an INCREASE: the dipole was in its lowest-energy orientation to begin with, so any reorientation can only raise its energy.

rows.stem:
(i) A thin spherical shell of radius R has a uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). Using Gauss' law, deduce an expression for electric field (i) outside and (ii) inside the shell.

(ii) Two long straight thin wires AB and CD have linear charge densities \(10\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\) and \(-20\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\), respectively. They are kept parallel to each other at a distance 1 m. Find magnitude and direction of the net electric field at a point midway between them.
rows.solution:
(i) Let the shell have radius R and uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\), so its total charge is \(Q = \sigma \times 4\pi R^{2}\). The charge distribution is spherically symmetric, so the field must be radial and of the same magnitude at every point of a concentric sphere. That is what makes Gauss's law usable.
(I) OUTSIDE THE SHELL, at \(r > R\). Take a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius r. It encloses the entire charge:
\(E \times 4\pi r^{2} = \dfrac{\sigma \times 4\pi R^{2}}{\varepsilon_{0}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = \dfrac{\sigma R^{2}}{\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\)
\(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma R^{2}}{\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\hat{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{Q}{r^{2}}\hat{r}\)
Outside, the shell behaves exactly as if its whole charge were concentrated at the centre.
(II) INSIDE THE SHELL, at \(r < R\). The Gaussian surface now lies entirely within the cavity, and since all the charge resides on the shell itself, the charge enclosed is ZERO:
\(E \times 4\pi r^{2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = 0\)
The field vanishes everywhere inside, which is the basis of electrostatic shielding.
(ii) The field of a long straight charged wire at distance r is \(E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\), and the midpoint is \(r = 0{\cdot}5\) m from each wire.
The directions are what make this add rather than subtract. AB carries a POSITIVE density, so its field at the midpoint points AWAY from AB, that is towards CD. CD carries a NEGATIVE density, so its field points TOWARDS CD as well. The two therefore point the same way and their magnitudes add:
\(E_{net} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\left[|\lambda_{1}| + |\lambda_{2}|\right] = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9}}{0{\cdot}5}\left[10 + 20\right] \times 10^{-6}\)
\(E_{net} = 1{\cdot}08 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\)
The net field is \(1{\cdot}08 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), directed from AB TOWARDS CD.

rows.stem:
(i) You are given three circuit elements X, Y and Z. They are connected one by one across a given ac source. It is found that V and I are in phase for element X. V leads I by \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) for element Y while I leads V by \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) for element Z. Identify elements X, Y and Z.

(ii) Establish the expression for impedance of circuit when elements X, Y and Z are connected in series to an ac source. Show the variation of current in the circuit with the frequency of the applied ac source.

(iii) In a series LCR circuit, obtain the conditions under which (i) impedance is minimum and (ii) wattless current flows in the circuit.
rows.solution:
(i) The phase relationship identifies each element.
X: V and I are IN PHASE, which is the behaviour of a pure RESISTOR.
Y: V LEADS I, which happens when the element is INDUCTIVE. The lead is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) rather than the \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) of an ideal inductor, so Y is a real inductor, one whose winding resistance happens to equal its reactance.
Z: I LEADS V, the signature of a CAPACITIVE element, again with a resistive part since the angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
(ii) IMPEDANCE OF THE SERIES COMBINATION. In series the same current flows through all three, so take the current as the reference phasor. The voltage across the resistor is in phase with it; the voltage across the inductor leads it by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\); the voltage across the capacitor lags it by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The last two are therefore in ANTIPHASE and combine to \(V_{C} - V_{L}\) along one line, at right angles to \(V_{R}\).
By Pythagoras on the phasor diagram:
\(V_{m}^{2} = V_{Rm}^{2} + (V_{Cm} - V_{Lm})^{2} = (i_{m}R)^{2} + (i_{m}X_{C} - i_{m}X_{L})^{2}\)
\(Z = \dfrac{V_{m}}{i_{m}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{C} - X_{L})^{2}}\)
VARIATION OF CURRENT WITH FREQUENCY. Plot \(i_{m}\) against \(\omega\). The curve rises from a small value at low frequency, where \(X_{C}\) is huge, passes through a sharp PEAK at the resonant frequency \(\omega_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), where the impedance falls to R, and falls away again at high frequency, where \(X_{L}\) dominates. A smaller resistance gives a taller, sharper peak.
(iii) (i) MINIMUM IMPEDANCE. From \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{C} - X_{L})^{2}}\) the smallest possible value is reached when the bracket vanishes:
\(X_{C} = X_{L} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Z_{min} = R\)
This is the condition of RESONANCE, and the current is then the largest it can be.
(ii) WATTLESS CURRENT. The average power over a cycle is \(P = VI\cos\phi\). A wattless current is one that transports no average power, so \(P = 0\) while V and I are both non-zero, which requires
\(\cos\phi = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
The circuit must be purely reactive, that is \(R = 0\). Energy is then merely shuttled back and forth between the source and the field of the inductor or capacitor, and none is dissipated.

rows.stem:
(i) Describe the construction and working of a transformer and hence obtain the relation for \(\left(\frac{v_s}{v_p}\right)\) in terms of number of turns of primary and secondary.

(ii) Discuss four main causes of energy loss in a real transformer.
rows.solution:
(i) CONSTRUCTION. A transformer consists of two coils, the PRIMARY of \(N_{P}\) turns and the SECONDARY of \(N_{S}\) turns, insulated from each other and wound on a common SOFT IRON core. They may be wound one on top of the other, or on separate limbs of the core. The core is LAMINATED, and soft iron is chosen for its high permeability so that almost all the flux produced by one coil threads the other.
WORKING. An alternating voltage applied to the primary drives an alternating current, which produces an alternating magnetic flux in the core. The core guides that flux through the secondary, where the changing flux induces an emf. Nothing passes between the coils but the flux; they are not electrically connected, which is why a transformer also provides isolation. A transformer works only on ac, since a steady current would give a constant flux and induce nothing.
If \(\phi\) is the flux linked with each turn, then
\(\varepsilon_{P} = V_{P} = -N_{P}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
\(\varepsilon_{S} = V_{S} = -N_{S}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \qquad\text{...(2)}\)
Dividing (2) by (1), the common factor \(\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\) cancels:
\(\dfrac{V_{S}}{V_{P}} = \dfrac{N_{S}}{N_{P}}\)
More turns on the secondary step the voltage UP, fewer step it DOWN. For an ideal transformer the power is unchanged, so the current changes in the inverse ratio.
(ii) FOUR CAUSES OF ENERGY LOSS in a real transformer:
- FLUX LEAKAGE. Not all the flux produced by the primary reaches the secondary, since the core cannot confine it perfectly. Reduced by winding the coils one over the other on a well-designed core.
- COPPER LOSS, the resistance of the windings. The currents dissipate \(I^{2}R\) as heat in the copper. Reduced by using thick wire of low resistance.
- EDDY CURRENTS, or iron loss. The changing flux induces circulating currents in the body of the core itself, which heat it. Reduced by LAMINATING the core, so the currents are confined to thin sheets.
- HYSTERESIS. The core is taken round a magnetisation cycle with every cycle of the supply, and the energy lost per cycle is the area of the hysteresis loop. Reduced by choosing a soft magnetic material such as soft iron, whose loop is narrow.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem:
(i) A plane light wave propagating from a rarer into a denser medium, is incident at an angle i on the surface separating two media. Using Huygen's principle, draw the refracted wave and hence verify Snell's law of refraction.

(ii) In a Young's double slit experiment, the slits are separated by 0.30 mm and the screen is kept 1.5 m away. The wavelength of light used is 600 nm. Calculate the distance between the central bright fringe and the 4th dark fringe.
rows.solution:
(i) Let a plane wavefront AB travel through medium 1 at speed \(v_{1}\) and meet the boundary PP' at an angle of incidence i. Medium 2 is denser, so light travels through it more slowly, at \(v_{2} < v_{1}\).
HUYGENS' CONSTRUCTION. Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. The wavefront meets the surface at A first, and the far end B has still to travel the distance BC before it arrives. If that takes a time \(\tau\), then
\(BC = v_{1}\tau\)
During the same time \(\tau\), the wavelet starting at A has spread INTO the second medium, travelling the shorter distance
\(AE = v_{2}\tau\)
Draw a sphere of radius \(v_{2}\tau\) about A and draw the tangent from C to it. That tangent plane CE is the REFRACTED WAVEFRONT, and the refracted rays are perpendicular to it, making an angle r with the normal.
VERIFICATION OF SNELL'S LAW. In the right-angled triangles ABC and AEC, which share the hypotenuse AC:
\(\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_{1}\tau}{AC}, \qquad \sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_{2}\tau}{AC}\)
Dividing, AC and \(\tau\) both cancel:
\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}\)
Writing the refractive indices as \(n_{1} = \dfrac{c}{v_{1}}\) and \(n_{2} = \dfrac{c}{v_{2}}\), this becomes
\(n_{1}\sin i = n_{2}\sin r\)
which is Snell's law. The construction also explains WHY the ray bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium: the part of the wavefront that arrives first is slowed first, so the front pivots.
(ii) The DARK fringes lie where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths:
\(x_{n} = \dfrac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d}\)
For the FOURTH dark fringe, \(n = 4\), with \(\lambda = 600\) nm, \(D = 1{\cdot}5\) m and \(d = 0{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{mm} = 0{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-3}\) m:
\(x_{4} = \dfrac{(2 \times 4 - 1) \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{2 \times 0{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{7 \times 9 \times 10^{-7}}{6 \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(x_{4} = 1{\cdot}05 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} = 10{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{mm}\)
The fourth dark fringe lies \(10{\cdot}5\) mm from the central bright fringe. As a check, the fringe width is \(\beta = 3\) mm and the fourth dark fringe should sit at \(3{\cdot}5\beta = 10{\cdot}5\) mm, which it does.

rows.stem:
(i) Discuss briefly diffraction of light from a single slit and draw the shape of the diffraction pattern.

(ii) An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. Using mirror formula, prove mathematically that it produces a virtual and an enlarged image.
rows.solution:
(i) DIFFRACTION AT A SINGLE SLIT. When a parallel beam of light falls normally on a narrow slit, the light does not travel on as a sharp-edged beam but spreads into the region behind the slit's edges. This bending is DIFFRACTION.
The pattern is explained by treating every point of the wavefront in the slit as a source of secondary wavelets, in Huygens' manner, and adding their contributions at each point of the screen. Straight ahead all the wavelets travel equal distances, arrive in phase and reinforce, giving a bright CENTRAL MAXIMUM. Away from the centre the wavelets from different parts of the slit arrive with a spread of phases. When the extra path across the whole slit is a whole wavelength, the wavelets cancel exactly in pairs and a MINIMUM appears, at
\(a\sin\theta = n\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
Between successive minima the cancellation is incomplete and weak SECONDARY MAXIMA appear.
SHAPE OF THE PATTERN. Sketch intensity against position on the screen: a tall broad central peak, twice as wide as any other, flanked on both sides by minima and by secondary maxima that fall away rapidly, the first being only a few per cent of the central intensity.
(ii) For a mirror, \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}\), which rearranges to
\(v = \dfrac{uf}{u - f}\)
Apply the Cartesian sign convention for a CONCAVE mirror with the object between the pole and the focus. Both the object distance and the focal length are measured against the incident light, so both are negative: replace u by \(-u\) and f by \(-f\), where now u and f stand for positive magnitudes.
\(v = \dfrac{(-u)(-f)}{(-u) - (-f)} = \dfrac{uf}{f - u}\)
The object lies NEARER than the focus, so \(u < f\) and the denominator \(f - u\) is POSITIVE. Hence v is positive.
A positive image distance means the image lies BEHIND the mirror, where no light actually goes, so the image is VIRTUAL.
For the size, the magnification is
\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\dfrac{uf}{f-u} = \dfrac{f}{f - u}\)
Since \(f - u\) is positive and smaller than f, the fraction exceeds 1:
\(m > 1\)
so the image is ENLARGED, and the positive sign makes it erect. A concave mirror used this way is a shaving or make-up mirror, which is exactly the everyday case of an object held closer than the focus.
